vignette:
Chidera is a thirty-five-year-old tutor who came to therapy at the urging of her partner, after nearly a year of what she described as "falling apart slowly." She is a tall, composed woman who speaks with careful precision, but her hands tremble slightly as she describes the night that changed everything. The rape happened eighteen months ago, on an evening she had been looking forward to. She had spent the day tutoring a young boy named Marcus, whose mother had just started a new job and was grateful for the extra help. Marcus was six, bright and affectionate, and Chidera had always enjoyed their sessions. That evening, after Marcus had gone to bed, his mother's boyfriend returned home early. He had been drinking. Chidera does not want to describe what happened next in detail. She says the memory does not feel like it belongs to her. When she tries to tell the story, the words will not come. She can see the scene in fragments-the kitchen counter, the sound of a glass breaking, the weight of his hand on her shoulder-but she cannot arrange them into a sequence that makes sense. What she can describe, with painful clarity, is the terror. It returns every time she remembers, as fresh and overwhelming as it was that night. She feels it in her stomach first, a wave of nausea that rises without warning, and then her mind goes blank, and she is back there, helpless, unable to speak.

In the weeks after the assault, Chidera tried to go on as usual. She returned to tutoring, but she found herself avoiding the homes of younger children. The sound of a child crying-any child, anywhere-would send a spike of dread through her chest. She began to associate that sound with the evening of the rape, though she could not explain why. It was the uncertainty that undid her. The moment she heard a child cry, she would freeze, waiting for something terrible to happen, her mind racing through possibilities she could not name. She started to cancel sessions with families who had babies or toddlers, inventing excuses about scheduling conflicts. Her income dropped, but she told herself it was temporary.

The self-blame was relentless. She would lie awake at night, replaying the evening, finding new reasons to fault herself. She should have left as soon as she saw the boyfriend's car. She should not have stayed to help Marcus finish his homework. She should have screamed louder. She should have fought. She repeated these thoughts so often that they became a kind of ritual, a way of staying in control by punishing herself for what she could not have prevented. She became convinced that she had been permanently damaged. She looked at herself in the mirror and did not recognize the person staring back. She was certain that the woman she had been-the one who laughed easily, who trusted people, who planned weekend trips with her partner-was gone forever.

She stopped accepting invitations to anything that might make her feel happy or hopeful. Birthdays, dinner parties, even a quiet evening at home with a movie she had been looking forward to-she turned them all down. Hope felt dangerous. It felt like a trap. If she let herself feel good, she reasoned, she would only be caught off guard when something terrible happened again. Her partner grew worried. He tried to talk to her, but whenever he brought up the assault, she would shut down. She could not bear to be reminded. She told him, with quiet desperation, that if she thought about the event too much, she would not be able to handle it. She would fall apart completely, and there would be no coming back.

Her tolerance for even the smallest upsets vanished. A missed bus, a late payment, a slightly harsh word from a student's parent-each one felt catastrophic. She would retreat to her bedroom, curl up on the floor, and wait for the feeling to pass. It never really did. The nausea stayed with her, a constant companion. She began to associate the feeling of being nauseous with the memory of that night, and so the nausea itself became a trigger. She was trapped in a loop she could not name.

What finally brought Chidera to therapy was a session with a new student. The child was seven, quiet, and reminded her of Marcus. She made it through the hour, but as she was leaving, the child's younger sibling started crying in the next room. Chidera froze in the hallway. She could not move. The mother found her standing there, tears streaming down her face, unable to explain why. Her partner drove her home, and that night, she agreed to make an appointment. She is terrified of what she might find in therapy-afraid that talking about the memory will break her, afraid that she is already broken. But she is also, beneath the fear, hoping for something she cannot quite name. She wants to stop being afraid of her own life.
